post_body:
Quick check: can your SF-425 cash drawn number tie to the general ledger without a side spreadsheet?

Start with cash received. Then cumulative expenditures. Then unliquidated obligations.

If those three numbers need three different owners to explain them, the report is already carrying reconciliation risk.

For the Executive Director asking for spend-down status before a funder call:

The answer should not be "Finance is pulling it."

The answer should be a short sentence:

"The Clinic Capacity grant is 61% spent, personnel is behind plan, supplies are on track, and the next report is due July 30."

That is an operating answer. It tells you the number, the risk, and the next deadline in one breath.

Your donor CRM can know the funder contact and still miss the grant.

A grant has a period of performance, approved budget, reporting cadence, allowable cost rules, amendments, and closeout package.

A donor record was not designed to carry that shape.

When the grant is flattened into a gift note, the operating record has to be rebuilt later, right when the report needs numbers.

Release from restriction: the accounting entry that moves dollars from net assets with donor restrictions to net assets without donor restrictions when the condition is satisfied.

The trigger matters.

For a purpose restriction, show the approved activity happened.

For a time restriction, show the time period passed.

"We are close enough to spent down" is not a trigger.

Seven things to have ready when a federal program officer asks for status.

1. Award number and ALN.
2. Period of performance dates.
3. Approved budget by line.
4. Spend-down by line.
5. Last SF-425 submitted.
6. Open prior approvals or amendments.
7. Next performance report due date.

That list is not the audit binder. It is the conversation file.

If it takes half a day to assemble, the grant record is not current enough for normal management.

If you receive federal funds through a state agency or another nonprofit, read the subaward agreement before the kickoff meeting.

The pass-through entity has to identify the federal award information, including the Assistance Listing Number, award identification, and applicable compliance requirements.

Your calendar should copy those requirements directly from the agreement.

Do not wait for the first monitoring request to learn what passed through.

The 2 CFR 200 Audit Prep Checklist is built for the week when "audit prep" becomes too vague to be useful.

It walks through a working evidence set for federal awards:

- SEFA support
- allowable cost documentation
- procurement files under 2 CFR 200.318
- time-and-effort records
- subrecipient monitoring evidence
- closeout files

Free download: grantpipe.com/free/2-cfr-200-audit-prep-checklist.

Time-and-effort records are not payroll decoration.

Under 2 CFR 200.430, salaries charged to federal awards need records that reflect the actual work performed.

A payroll register proves someone was paid.

It does not prove which grant paid for which share of their time.

That second proof is where a clean-looking file can get thin.

Grants.gov is for finding and applying to federal opportunities.

Post-award reporting happens somewhere else.

SF-425s, drawdowns, performance reports, and closeout steps live in agency systems such as PMS, GrantSolutions, IDIS, DRGR, or JustGrants, depending on the award.

That distinction matters when you build a compliance calendar.

"Submitted in Grants.gov" is not the end of the operating record.

Restricted balance check:

Award amount received to date minus cumulative allowable expenditures should equal the remaining restricted balance.

If the accounting balance says something different, pause before month close.

The variance may be a miscoded receipt, an expense charged to the wrong fund, or a journal entry that moved dollars without enough support.

Small variances get expensive when they roll forward.

The Grant Spend-Down Tracker is for the question that comes before panic:

"Are we going to spend this grant correctly before the award ends?"

It tracks approved budget, actuals to date, remaining balance, percentage spent, and projected balance at award end.

It is not a pretty budget report. It is an early warning system.

Free download: grantpipe.com/free/grant-spend-down-tracker.

Development and Finance do not need another handoff spreadsheet.

They need fewer moments where the same grant is re-entered.

The funder contact belongs near the donor history.

The award terms belong near the budget.

The restricted fund belongs near the ledger.

The evidence belongs near the report.

When those records are split, the handoff becomes the control. That is too much pressure for email.

We modeled grants and funds as separate records in GrantPipe.

A grant is an agreement: funder, award amount, period, reports, amendments.

A fund is a pool of restricted dollars: balance, activity, releases, net asset classification.

They overlap, but they are not the same thing.

That choice made the product harder to build. It also prevents a bad shortcut: treating one grant as one fund forever.

Real restricted fund work is many-to-many. The data model has to admit that.

Board packet test:

Can the narrative paragraph about restricted funds tie to the financial statement line without a manual explanation?

The board may not ask for the schedule by fund.

The auditor may ask for it later.

Write the packet so both readers see the same story.

Closeout starts before the grant ends.

For federal awards, the closeout clock includes final financial reporting, final performance reporting, liquidation of obligations, and record retention.

Waiting until the last week turns closeout into archaeology.

Start with the grant agreement, the final approved budget, and the last spend-down report. Those three files tell you where to look next.

Friday close question:

Which grant report due next week would fail if one person were out Monday?

If the answer is "none," good.

If the answer is a name, the risk is not that person. The risk is the missing backup trail.

Monthly reports go sideways when the same number has two homes.

Development has the funder-facing story.

Finance has the ledger.

Program has the activity data.

The report needs all three, but the reconciliation should not happen in the final draft.

Put the grant record together before writing. Numbers first, narrative second.

A clean closeout package answers five questions.

What was awarded?

What changed through amendments?

What was spent, by approved line?

What was delivered?

What evidence supports the spending and the delivery?

If those answers live in separate folders, closeout becomes a search project.

Board-safe numbers are boring in the best way.

They reconcile to the general ledger.

They match the restricted fund schedule.

They use the same grant names Finance uses.

They do not change between the ED narrative and the finance appendix.

If the board packet needs a footnote explaining why two totals differ, fix the totals before the meeting.

Four checks before you close the month on grant activity.

1. Bank deposits tie to grant receipts in the general ledger.
2. Grant expenses tie to the correct fund code.
3. Restricted balances match expected remaining balances.
4. Drawdowns are supported by posted expenditures.

That sequence is plain. It is also where the audit trail starts.

Do it monthly and year-end gets quieter.

The SF-425 has two different rhythms.

Quarterly reports are typically due 30 days after the quarter ends.

The final SF-425 is typically due 90 days after the grant period ends.

Do not put only one deadline on the calendar.

The final report is where unliquidated obligations, program income, and closeout documentation all come back for review.

The Donor-to-Grant Reconciliation Template is for the Friday problem:

The donor CRM says one thing. The general ledger says another. The grant tracker says a third.

The template gives Development and Finance one worksheet for gifts, grants, restrictions, fund codes, and report dates.

It is deliberately unglamorous.

Free download: grantpipe.com/free/donor-to-grant-reconciliation-template.

If you import a grant into your CRM, do not stop at the funder name and amount.

Minimum fields worth carrying:

- award ID
- period of performance
- approved budget version
- reporting cadence
- restriction purpose
- fund code
- next report owner

That is the difference between a contact note and a working grant record.

A restricted fund note should say more than "restricted."

Useful notes name the restriction:

"Clinic Capacity grant, personnel and equipment only, award period 2026-01-01 to 2026-12-31."

Even better: attach the source document, budget, and release trigger.

The label tells you to be careful. The evidence tells you what careful means.

ALN replaced CFDA as the federal assistance listing identifier.

If you receive a pass-through award, the ALN is not trivia. It tells auditors which federal program is behind the money.

Put it on the grant record.

Put it on the SEFA support file.

Put it in the folder name if that is what your team actually searches.

Tiny identifiers save real time during fieldwork.

Finance committee packets should carry one grant-specific page.

Not ten tabs.

One page:

- active grants
- next reporting deadline
- restricted balance
- spend-down risk
- open compliance items

The full board needs the story. The finance committee needs the control surface.

Give them the page that makes questions easier to ask.

The Auditor Evidence Checklist is a practical map of what to keep within reach:

- trial balance and general ledger
- bank reconciliations
- grant agreements
- submitted funder reports
- payroll and time records
- board minutes
- policies
- SEFA support where federal awards apply

Free download: grantpipe.com/free/auditor-evidence-checklist.

One record should answer two questions.

For Development: who funded this work, why did they care, and what relationship needs stewardship?

For Finance: what restriction governs the dollars, what has been spent, and what report is due?

That is the donor plus grant problem.

The same award has a relationship side and an accounting side. Splitting them guarantees a reconciliation habit.

We publish GrantPipe pricing because early trust should not require a sales call.

The current source of truth:

Starter: $39/mo billed annually.
Growth: $79/mo billed annually.
Audit Ready: $159/mo billed annually.

Unlimited users. One-month free trial. No credit card to start. No setup fee.

There is enough uncertainty in choosing new software. The price should not be part of it.

Time records are easier to fix on Friday than during audit week.

Before you close the week, pick one federally funded employee and check:

Does the record show actual work performed?

Does it tie to the grant or cost objective?

Is it signed or approved according to policy?

One spot check a week beats one panic sweep a year.

Saturday operating check:

Open the grant calendar and look only 30 days ahead.

Reports. Drawdowns. Board approvals. Renewal decisions. Closeout dates.

Do not reorganize the system.

Move one unclear owner to a named owner. That is enough useful work for a quiet morning.

Restricted fund cleanup can be small.

Pick one fund.

Find the source document.

Write the restriction in one plain sentence.

Check the current balance.

Name the release trigger.

That is not a full reconciliation. It is a better record than yesterday.

The shared drive is not the evidence trail.

It can store the evidence. It cannot explain the story by itself.

An auditor opening a folder still needs to know which document supports which report, which expense, which amendment, and which release.

That link has to live somewhere more precise than "Grants 2026 final final."

UEI cleanup is a decent weekend task.

Check that the UEI on your SAM.gov registration matches the UEI on current federal award documents and pass-through agreements.

Then check who owns the renewal calendar.

The work is administrative, but the cost of a stale registration is operational. It can slow applications, amendments, and payments.

Six files worth finding before audit season.

1. Trial balance.
2. Full general ledger export.
3. Bank reconciliations.
4. Grant agreements and amendments.
5. Submitted financial reports.
6. Board minutes for budget and grant approvals.

Do not polish them first.

Find them. Name them. Put them where next week's version of you can find them again.

The Auditor Evidence Checklist is useful before the auditor asks.

It names the core document categories: GL, trial balance, bank recs, grant agreements, payroll records, board minutes, policies, and SEFA support.

Use it as a gap scan while there is still time to fix the folders.

Free download: grantpipe.com/free/auditor-evidence-checklist.

A donor stewardship calendar is mostly a promise to your future self.

Thank-you notes.

Mid-year updates.

Report mail dates.

Board introductions.

Renewal asks.

You can keep it in a spreadsheet, a CRM, or a notebook. The tool matters less than the habit: every relationship with a next step, and every next step with an owner.

Period of performance is the date range that decides whether a cost belongs on a federal grant.

Not the invoice date alone.

Not the payment date alone.

The work has to be incurred inside the approved period, with liquidation and reporting handled inside the closeout rules.

When you review old invoices, read the service dates first.

Board-designated is not donor-restricted.

A board can set aside dollars for a building reserve, operating cushion, or future program.

That internal designation still sits inside net assets without donor restrictions under FASB ASC 958.

Donor restrictions come from outside the organization. Board designations come from governance.

Mixing those two makes financial statements harder to read.

A CRM migration map should include the grant data the CRM did not really hold.

Do not map only contacts, gifts, and notes.

Map funder records, grant IDs, award terms, restriction purposes, fund codes, reporting deadlines, and document locations.

Otherwise the migration looks complete on donor day one and incomplete on grant report day thirty.

Saturday reminder for Development Directors:

Cleaning the database can be real work.

Avoiding donor calls by cleaning the database is something else.

Pick one useful cleanup task and one human task.

Merge five duplicates.

Then send one note to a donor who funded something specific and has not heard the outcome yet.

Procurement files are easier to build when the purchase happens.

For federal awards, 2 CFR 200.318 sets the general procurement standards.

A clean file can include the purchase request, quotes or selection memo, conflict check, approval, invoice, and proof the cost was charged to the right award.

If the purchase is already in the ledger but the procurement trail is still in inboxes, fix that before fieldwork.

The Cost Allocation Plan Worksheet is for shared costs that refuse to stay in one neat bucket.

Rent. Utilities. Finance staff time. Software. Insurance.

The worksheet prompts the allocation base, the calculation, the approval trail, and the grant restrictions that affect the charge.

Free download: grantpipe.com/free/cost-allocation-plan-worksheet.

review_notes: no fabricated proof Final consolidation replaced proof-risk wording with permission-safe wording.
post_body:
We will not make up proof for GrantPipe.

That means no invented customer quotes, no customer names without permission, no borrowed authority, and no pretending a young product has history it has not earned.

The trade is simple: fewer easy marketing lines, more honest product work.

That is the only way I know to build software that can sit near audits, restricted funds, and board reports without feeling unserious.

Sunday starts better when Saturday ends clean.

Close the tabs you opened to avoid the real task.

Write the three things Monday needs from you.

Name one grant report, one donor follow-up, and one finance question.

Then stop.

Nonprofit operating work expands into every quiet hour unless someone gives it a boundary.

Sunday prep:

Open the week ahead and look for the handoffs, not the deadlines.

Who needs a number from Finance?

Who needs a narrative from Program?

Who needs a signature from the ED?

A clean handoff makes the deadline less fragile. Start there.

Monday handoff test:

Can Development tell Finance which new gifts are restricted before Finance closes the deposits?

Can Finance tell Development which grant balances changed before the funder update is drafted?

Two small yeses prevent a week of cleanup.

If you only prepare three audit files this weekend, make them these:

1. Trial balance tied to the general ledger.
2. Bank reconciliations signed and dated.
3. Grant agreement folder with awards and amendments.

Those files anchor the rest of the audit conversation.

Everything else gets easier when the anchors are findable.

The Audit Prep Week-by-Week Checklist is built for teams that need a sequence, not another giant request list.

It breaks prep into weekly passes:

- evidence inventory
- grant files
- payroll and time records
- board and policy documents
- final PBC response review

Free download: grantpipe.com/free/audit-prep-week-by-week-checklist.

Five board questions to answer before Monday.

What changed in cash?

Which restricted balances are aging?

Which grant reports are due before the next meeting?

Which renewal decisions need board context?

Which budget variance needs a plain-English explanation?

The board packet should not bury those answers. It should make them impossible to miss.

A release schedule is a promise to explain later.

For each restricted fund, write:

- source
- restriction purpose
- amount released this period
- evidence for the release
- remaining balance

That schedule does not need drama.

It needs to reconcile to the statement of activities and survive the question: "Why did this release happen now?"

GrantPipe includes Grants.gov federal opportunity search.

That is the searchable federal source.

Non-federal opportunities can be tracked manually or imported from CSV. Foundation prospect context can use public nonprofit filings where available.

That boundary matters.

We are not claiming a proprietary private foundation database. We are building the operating record around opportunities, awards, restrictions, reports, and evidence.

Donor-to-grant reconciliation starts with one blunt question:

Which dollars in the donor system created restrictions in the finance system?

If that link is fuzzy, every later report gets harder.

The thank-you letter, the restricted fund schedule, and the funder report are not separate stories. They are different views of the same commitment.

A useful development calendar shows more than asks.

It shows stewardship dates, board introductions, grant reports, renewal windows, thank-you letter batches, and finance handoffs.

When a funder relationship also has stewardship work, the calendar should show both.

Put them where the collisions are visible.

The Award Setup Worksheet is a first-30-days document.

Use it when the grant is awarded, before the details scatter:

- funder and award ID
- period of performance
- approved budget
- reporting cadence
- indirect cost treatment
- restriction purpose
- owner for each deadline

Free download: grantpipe.com/free/award-setup-worksheet.

Public pricing is a product decision.

So is month-to-month billing.

So is no setup fee.

So is a one-month trial that starts without a credit card.

GrantPipe is still early. That means buyers deserve fewer hidden variables, not more.

When the product is new, the terms should be plain.

Questioned cost: a cost an auditor or federal reviewer flags because it may not be allowable, allocable, reasonable, or supported.

It is not automatically a repayment.

It is a demand for evidence.

The best time to prepare that evidence is when the cost is charged, not when the question arrives.

The Donor Retention Dashboard Template is not grant compliance content, and that is the point.

Development leaders still need a clean view of:

- retained donors
- lapsed donors
- new donors
- recurring donors
- upgrade opportunities

A grant calendar still has a relationship side.

Free download: grantpipe.com/free/donor-retention-dashboard-template.

I would rather say "we are early" than pretend GrantPipe has proof it has not earned.

Early means public pricing.

Early means a trial that can run on the buyer's own data, not a staged demo.

Early means writing down the product boundaries, including Grants.gov search for federal opportunities and manual or imported tracking for non-federal ones.

Trust starts with not overstating the product.

Before Monday starts, write the three lists.

Due this week.

Waiting on someone else.

Needs a decision.

That is enough structure for a nonprofit operating week.

Not perfect. Not fancy. Enough to keep the first meeting from becoming a scavenger hunt.
